irdabama.name: Irdabama
irdabama.summary: The wealthiest known businesswoman recorded in the Achaemenid Empire's Persepolis archives, active during the reign of Darius the Great, dealing mainly in wine and grain and overseeing estates across the empire.

darius-the-great.name: Darius the Great
darius-the-great.summary: Third King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire (522–486 BCE), who ruled it at its territorial peak, reorganized it into provinces, and commissioned the Behistun inscription.

persepolis.name: Persepolis
persepolis.summary: Ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, built from about 515 BC in what is now Fars province, Iran; its palaces were burned after Alexander the Great's army captured it in 330 BC.

shiraz.name: Shiraz
shiraz.summary: Iran's fifth-most-populous city and capital of Fars province, a regional trade center for over a thousand years and home to the poets Hafez and Saadi.

lloyd-llewellyn-jones.name: Lloyd Llewellyn-Jones
lloyd-llewellyn-jones.summary: A Welsh professor of ancient history specializing in ancient Iran's Achaemenid period, holding the Chair of Ancient History at Cardiff University since 2016.

fars-province.name: Fars province
fars-province.summary: A province in southwestern Iran, historically known as Persis, whose capital is the city of Shiraz.

khuzestan-province.name: Khuzestan province
khuzestan-province.summary: A province in southwestern Iran bordering Iraq and the Persian Gulf, corresponding to ancient Elam whose capital was Susa; it holds Iran's largest oil field.

firuzabad-fars.name: Firuzabad
firuzabad-fars.summary: A city in Iran's Fars province on the site of the ancient city of Gor, revived by Sasanian founder Ardashir I after Alexander the Great had destroyed the original settlement.

bishapur.name: Bishapur
bishapur.summary: An ancient Iranian city founded in 266 CE by Shapur I to commemorate a Sasanian victory over Rome, remaining important until the Muslim conquest of Persia.

ctesiphon.name: Ctesiphon
ctesiphon.summary: An ancient city on the Tigris near modern Baghdad that served as capital of the Parthian and Sasanian Persian empires for over 800 years, until falling in the 637 Muslim conquest.

achaemenid-empire.name: Achaemenid Empire
achaemenid-empire.summary: Ancient Iranian empire founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BC, the largest of its time, stretching from the Balkans to the Indus Valley before Alexander the Great conquered it in 330 BC.

shapur-i.name: Shapur I
shapur-i.summary: Second Sasanian King of Kings of Iran, ruling from 240 to 270 CE, who expanded the empire and defeated two Roman emperors, capturing Valerian in 260.

avestan.name: Avestan
avestan.summary: The liturgical language of Zoroastrianism, an Iranian branch of Indo-European spoken from about 1500 to 400 BCE and closely related to Vedic Sanskrit.

old-persian.name: Old Persian
old-persian.summary: An ancient Iranian language attested in inscriptions and tablets of the Achaemenid era (about 600–300 BCE), most notably the Behistun Inscription.

median-language.name: Median language
median-language.summary: An extinct Northwestern Iranian language spoken by the ancient Medes, thought to be ancestral to later languages such as Gilaki, Mazanderani, Talysh and Zaza.

xerxes-i.name: Xerxes I
xerxes-i.summary: Persian king (c. 518-465 BC) who ruled the Achaemenid Empire from 486 BC, famed for his 480 BC invasion of Greece that won early victories but ended in defeat at Salamis and Plataea.

artaxerxes-i.name: Artaxerxes I
artaxerxes-i.summary: The fifth King of Kings of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, ruling from 465 to 424 BC; some traditions identify him with King Ahasuerus of the Book of Esther.

darius-ii.name: Darius II
darius-ii.summary: Achaemenid King of Kings from 423 to 405/404 BC, born Ochus, who took the throne after a succession struggle and faced repeated revolts by satraps.

alexander-the-great.name: Alexander the Great
alexander-the-great.summary: King of Macedon from 336 BC who conquered much of the known world by age 30, creating an empire stretching from Greece to India; tutored by Aristotle.

ziwiye-hoard.name: Ziwiye hoard
ziwiye-hoard.summary: A treasure hoard of gold, silver and ivory objects, including gold pieces shaped like human faces, found near Saqqez in Iran's Kurdistan province in 1947.

teppe-hasanlu.name: Hasanlu
teppe-hasanlu.summary: An ancient city site in Iran near Lake Urmia, famous for the Golden Bowl of Hasanlu, whose destruction around the 9th century BC preserved one layer of the city intact.

squinch.name: Squinch
squinch.summary: An architectural element that supports a round or octagonal dome on a square base, originating in Sassanid Persia and later used in Islamic, Georgian and Armenian buildings.

darreh-shahr-ancient-city.name: Madaktu
darreh-shahr-ancient-city.summary: Ancient Elamite capital, remnants of which lie beneath the later Sasanian-era ruined city near modern Darreh Shahr in Iran's Ilam Province.

kul-e-farah.name: Kul-e Farah
kul-e-farah.summary: Open-air archaeological sanctuary in Iran's Zagros Mountains, home to six Elamite-era rock reliefs near the town of Izeh.

elam.name: Elam
elam.summary: An ancient civilization centered in western and southwestern Iran, one of the leading political forces of the ancient Near East, with written records from around 3000 BCE.

mu-u-u.name: Mušḫuššu
mu-u-u.summary: A mythological hybrid creature from ancient Mesopotamian mythology, with a scaly body, eagle-like talons, lion forelimbs, horns and a snake-like tongue; famously shown on Babylon's Ishtar Gate.

ishtar-gate.name: Ishtar Gate
ishtar-gate.summary: The eighth gate of Babylon's inner city wall, built around 569 BC under King Nebuchadnezzar II, decorated with glazed-brick animals and deities; excavated by Robert Koldewey from 1904 to 1914.

great-mosque-of-samarra.name: Great Mosque of Samarra
great-mosque-of-samarra.summary: A former congregational mosque in Samarra, Iraq, commissioned in 848 CE and completed in 851 by the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil; it was the world's largest mosque at the time.

cyrus-the-great.name: Cyrus the Great
cyrus-the-great.summary: Founder of the Achaemenid Empire (c. 600–530 BC), who conquered the Median, Lydian and Neo-Babylonian empires to create the largest empire of its time, known for tolerating local customs and religions.

media-region.name: Media
media-region.summary: An Iron Age region of northwestern Iran that served as the political and cultural base of the Medes, later becoming an Achaemenid satrapy stretching as far as southern Dagestan.

lydia.name: Lydia
lydia.summary: A wealthy Iron Age kingdom of western Anatolia (8th–6th centuries BC), capital Sardis, credited with the world's first coinage, which became a Persian satrapy in 546 BC.

neo-babylonian-empire.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
neo-babylonian-empire.summary: The last empire ruled by native Mesopotamian kings, from 626 to 539 BC, remembered for Nebuchadnezzar II's destruction of Jerusalem's Temple and a cultural renaissance in Babylon.

scythia.name: Scythia
scythia.summary: A geographic region of the ancient Graeco-Roman world covering the Pontic steppe, home to the Scythians, an ancient Eastern Iranic nomadic people.

darius-iii.name: Darius III
darius-iii.summary: Last Achaemenid King of Persia (336–330 BC), defeated by Alexander the Great in several battles before being killed by his own relative Bessus.

battle-of-issus.name: Battle of Issus
battle-of-issus.summary: A 333 BC battle in which Alexander the Great's forces defeated Darius III's Persian army, forcing Darius to flee and abandon his family and treasury.

battle-of-gaugamela.name: Battle of Gaugamela
battle-of-gaugamela.summary: The decisive 331 BC battle in which Alexander the Great's outnumbered army defeated Darius III's Persian forces, effectively ending the Achaemenid Empire.

miletus.name: Miletus
miletus.summary: Ancient Greek city on Anatolia's western coast, a wealthy maritime and trading power that founded dozens of Mediterranean and Black Sea colonies and was home to early philosophers such as Thales; known in Hittite records as Millawata.

sardis.name: Sardis
sardis.summary: An ancient city in what is now Turkey, capital of the Lydian Empire and later of a Persian satrapy, now an active archaeological site and UNESCO World Heritage Site.

greco-persian-wars.name: Greco-Persian Wars
greco-persian-wars.summary: A series of conflicts from 499 to 449 BC between Greek city-states and the Achaemenid Persian Empire, sparked by Persian rule over Ionia and the Ionian Revolt.

second-persian-invasion-of-greece.name: Second Persian invasion of Greece
second-persian-invasion-of-greece.summary: Persia's invasion of Greece from 480 to 479 BC under King Xerxes I, marked by the Battle of Thermopylae and ending in Greek victories at Salamis and Plataea.

isthmus-of-corinth.name: Isthmus of Corinth
isthmus-of-corinth.summary: The narrow land bridge linking the Peloponnese to mainland Greece near Corinth, long regarded as the boundary between the two and now cut by the Corinth Canal, built in 1893.

battle-of-plataea.name: Battle of Plataea
battle-of-plataea.summary: The final land battle of Persia's second invasion of Greece, fought in August 479 BC, in which a Spartan-led Greek alliance defeated the Achaemenid army of Mardonius, who was killed, ending Persia's foothold in mainland Greece.

battle-of-salamis.name: Battle of Salamis
battle-of-salamis.summary: A naval battle in 480 BC in which an outnumbered Greek fleet under Themistocles defeated King Xerxes' Achaemenid Persian fleet near Athens, marking a turning point in the Persian invasion of Greece.

amyrtaeus.name: Amyrtaeus
amyrtaeus.summary: The only pharaoh of Egypt's Twenty-eighth Dynasty, who ended the first Persian occupation of Egypt and reigned from 404 to 399 BC, beginning about 60 years of native rule.

artaxerxes-iii.name: Artaxerxes III
artaxerxes-iii.summary: King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire from 359/58 to 338 BC, who reconquered Egypt after two campaigns and began new building work at Persepolis before his assassination.

ardashir-i.name: Ardashir I
ardashir-i.summary: Founder of the Sasanian Empire (180–242 AD), who overthrew the Parthian Arsacid dynasty in 224 and took the title King of Kings, beginning ancient Iran's last pre-Islamic empire.

artabanus-iv-of-parthia.name: Artabanus IV
artabanus-iv-of-parthia.summary: The last monarch of the Parthian Empire, ruling from about 213 to 224 CE and also known as Artabanus V in older scholarship. He was defeated and killed by Ardashir I in 224, ending Parthian rule.

susiana.name: Susiana
susiana.summary: Ancient region in southwestern Iran around the city of Susa, forming the core lowland zone of early Elamite civilization and later organized as an Achaemenid satrapy.

characene.name: Mesene (Characene)
characene.summary: Also called Mesene, a kingdom at the head of the Persian Gulf in modern Iraq, often a vassal of the Parthian Empire.

mardonius-nephew-of-darius-i.name: Mardonius
mardonius-nephew-of-darius-i.summary: Persian military commander during the Greco-Persian Wars who led invasions of Greece under Darius I and Xerxes I, and was killed at the Battle of Plataea in 479 BC.

thrace.name: Thrace
thrace.summary: A historical and geographical region in Southeast Europe, roughly matching the Roman province of Thrace, spanning parts of modern Bulgaria, Greece and Turkey.

delian-league.name: Delian League
delian-league.summary: A confederacy of Greek city-states founded in 478 BC under Athenian leadership to continue fighting Persia after the victory at Plataea; it later became an Athenian naval empire.

peace-of-callias.name: Peace of Callias
peace-of-callias.summary: A disputed peace treaty said to have been agreed around 449 BCE between Athens's Delian League and Achaemenid Persia, ending the Greco-Persian Wars and giving autonomy to Greek cities in Asia Minor.

artaxerxes-ii.name: Artaxerxes II
artaxerxes-ii.summary: King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire from 405/4 to 359/8 BC, who defeated his brother Cyrus the Younger's revolt and later faced further rebellions.

corinthian-war.name: Corinthian War
corinthian-war.summary: A conflict from 395 to 387 BC in which Sparta fought a coalition of Thebes, Athens, Corinth, and Argos, backed for a time by the Achaemenid Persian Empire.

ionia.name: Ionia
ionia.summary: An ancient region on the central western coast of Anatolia settled by Greek Ionians, home to twelve cities of the Ionian League and central to conflicts between Persia and Greece.

aeolis.name: Aeolis
aeolis.summary: A region on the coast of northwestern Asia Minor, home to Aeolian Greek city-states and islands including Lesbos.

avesta.name: Avesta
avesta.summary: The corpus of religious texts of Zoroastrianism, composed orally over centuries before being written down under the Sasanians and later largely lost after the Islamic conquest of Iran.

gathas.name: Gathas
gathas.summary: The central hymns of Zoroastrianism, traditionally attributed to Zarathustra and composed in the oldest attested Iranian language, among the oldest surviving Indo-European texts.

zoroaster.name: Zoroaster
zoroaster.summary: Iranian religious reformer traditionally dated to the 7th-6th centuries BC (some scholars place him earlier), who became the spiritual founder of Zoroastrianism through his hymns, the Gathas.

behistun-inscription.name: Behistun inscription
behistun-inscription.summary: A multilingual Achaemenid rock inscription and relief carved for Darius the Great between 522 and 486 BCE, key to deciphering cuneiform as the longest known trilingual inscription.

parthian-language.name: Parthian language
parthian-language.summary: An extinct Northwestern Iranian language once spoken in Parthia, serving as the state language of the Parthian Empire and shaping much of Armenian vocabulary.

middle-persian.name: Middle Persian
middle-persian.summary: A Western Iranian language that became the literary language of the Sasanian Empire and is the linguistic ancestor of modern Persian.

nowzar.name: Nowzar
nowzar.summary: The ninth legendary Shah of Persia's Pishdadian dynasty, according to the Shahnameh, who ruled seven years before being killed in battle by Afrasiab.

khorasan.name: Khorasan
khorasan.summary: A historical region of the Iranian Plateau spanning parts of modern Afghanistan, Iran and Central Asia, with boundaries that varied over time and roots reaching back to Bronze Age complex societies there.

vishtaspa.name: Vishtaspa
vishtaspa.summary: Figure in Zoroastrian tradition portrayed as an early follower and royal patron of Zoroaster who helped spread his teachings; traditionally considered a historical king, though obscured by legend.

zoroastrianism.name: Zoroastrianism
zoroastrianism.summary: An ancient Iranian religion founded on the teachings of Zoroaster, centred on the deity Ahura Mazda and the choice between truth and chaos, once Greater Iran's dominant faith under the Sassanid Empire.

academy-of-gondishapur.name: Academy of Gondishapur
academy-of-gondishapur.summary: A Sassanid-era center of learning in Iran with a hospital and library, founded by King Shapur I and considered among history's oldest universities.

vendidad.name: Vendidad
vendidad.summary: The only volume of the Sasanian Avesta still present in the extant Avesta collection, a Zoroastrian text likely preserved through its use in liturgy.

sais-egypt.name: Sais
sais-egypt.summary: Ancient Egyptian city in the western Nile Delta that became the seat of power during the 24th Dynasty (c. 732–720 BC) and the Saite 26th Dynasty (664–525 BC).

emilie-savage-smith.name: Emilie Savage-Smith
emilie-savage-smith.summary: An American-British historian born in 1941, known for her research on science and medicine in the medieval Islamic world.

herodotus.name: Herodotus
herodotus.summary: Greek historian and geographer (c. 484–c. 425 BC), called 'the Father of History' for his Histories, a detailed account of the Greco-Persian Wars and the peoples and lands around them.

persis.name: Persis
persis.summary: A historical region in south-western Iran, roughly today's Fars province, where migrating Iranian-speaking peoples settled in the early 1st millennium BC and became known as Persians.

cyrenaica.name: Cyrenaica
cyrenaica.summary: Eastern region of Libya named for the ancient city of Cyrene, once part of the Roman province of Crete and Cyrenaica and later Libya's Barqa region under Islamic rule.

battle-of-hormozdgan.name: Battle of Hormozdgan
battle-of-hormozdgan.summary: The battle of 28 April 224 in which the Sasanians defeated the Parthian Arsacid dynasty, ending nearly five centuries of Parthian rule and marking the start of the Sasanian era.

sasanian-dynasty.name: Sasanian dynasty
sasanian-dynasty.summary: The ruling family of the Sasanian Empire, founded by Ardashir I in 224 CE and named for his ancestor Sasan; after the 651 Muslim conquest, exiled members took refuge at the Chinese imperial court.

parthian-empire.name: Parthian Empire
parthian-empire.summary: A major Iranian empire ruled by the Arsacid dynasty, lasting from 247 BC to 224 AD and stretching from the Euphrates to Afghanistan.

arsaces-i-of-parthia.name: Arsaces I
arsaces-i-of-parthia.summary: First king of Parthia, ruling from 247 to 217 BC, and founder of the Arsacid dynasty that later grew into the Parthian Empire.

bagoas-courtier.name: Bagoas
bagoas-courtier.summary: A eunuch at the 4th-century BC Persian royal court, serving first Darius III and then Alexander the Great.

arses-of-persia.name: Arses
arses-of-persia.summary: Twelfth Achaemenid King of Kings, ruling 338 to 336 BC under the regnal name Artaxerxes IV; placed on the throne and later poisoned by the eunuch Bagoas.

delos.name: Delos
delos.summary: A tiny Greek island near Mykonos revered as the mythical birthplace of Apollo and Artemis, sacred for a millennium and now a major archaeological site.

cyaxares.name: Cyaxares
cyaxares.summary: Third king of the Medes, who took the throne in 625 BC, overthrew Scythian domination, and allied with Babylon to destroy the Assyrian Empire, turning Media into a major power.

medes.name: Medes
medes.summary: An Iron Age Iranian people who inhabited northwestern Iran from around the 11th century BCE and, according to Greek sources, formed a powerful state that helped overthrow the Assyrian Empire.

median-kingdom.name: Median Empire
median-kingdom.summary: A polity centered on Ecbatana from the 7th to mid-6th century BCE that, allied with Babylonia, helped overthrow the Neo-Assyrian Empire and expanded under Cyaxares to form what is called the first Iranian empire.

noushijan.name: Noushijan
noushijan.summary: An archaeological site in western Iran, occupied from around 800 BC, with remains including a fire temple, a columned hall, and a central temple.

inaros-ii.name: Inaros II
inaros-ii.summary: Egyptian rebel ruler who revolted against the Persians in 460 BC with Athenian help, defeating a Persian army before being captured and crucified at Susa in 454 BC.

achaemenes-satrap.name: Achaemenes
achaemenes-satrap.summary: An Achaemenid general and satrap of Egypt in the early 5th century BC, during the time of Egypt's 27th Dynasty.

megabyzus.name: Megabyzus
megabyzus.summary: Achaemenid Persian general who recaptured Babylon after its revolt in 484 BCE and later fought in the Second Persian invasion of Greece (480–479 BCE).

susa.name: Susa
susa.summary: Ancient city in what is now Iran that served as capital of Elam and winter capital of the Achaemenid Empire, remaining strategically important through the Parthian and Sasanian periods.

house-of-suren.name: House of Suren
house-of-suren.summary: A noble Parthian family who ruled Sistan and held major influence within the Parthian Empire, one of only two families named explicitly in sources from that era.

house-of-karen.name: House of Karen
house-of-karen.summary: One of the Seven Great Houses of Iran under the Parthian and Sasanian Empires, seated at Nahavand near Ecbatana, holding high administrative rank for centuries.

house-of-varaz.name: House of Varaz
house-of-varaz.summary: A family of the Sasanian Empire recorded in third-century inscriptions at the courts of several shahs, though later sources rarely mention them by name.

shah.name: Shahanshah
shah.summary: Meaning 'king of kings,' this elevated title was used by Iranian monarchs from the Achaemenid dynasty onward, marking them as successors to Cyrus the Great's empire.

stateira-wife-of-artaxerxes-ii.name: Stateira
stateira-wife-of-artaxerxes-ii.summary: An Achaemenid queen, chief consort of Persian king Artaxerxes II and mother of his successor Artaxerxes III, until her death around 400 BC.

parysatis.name: Parysatis
parysatis.summary: A Persian queen, consort of Darius II, who wielded major influence during the reign of her son Artaxerxes II.

aspasia-of-phocaea.name: Aspasia of Phocaea
aspasia-of-phocaea.summary: A Greek woman from Phocaea taken into the harem of Cyrus the Younger, who made her his favorite wife; after his death at Cunaxa she became a wife of Artaxerxes II.

phocaea.name: Phocaea
phocaea.summary: Ancient Ionian Greek city on the western coast of Anatolia that founded the colonies of Massalia (Marseille), Emporion and Elea.

artabanus-of-persia.name: Artabanus
artabanus-of-persia.summary: A Persian political figure under the Achaemenid dynasty who was reportedly the power behind the throne for a few months around 465 BC.

church-of-the-east.name: Church of the East
church-of-the-east.summary: An Eastern Christian branch, also called the Nestorian Church, that arose from 5th-century Christological disputes and originated in Mesopotamia under the Parthian Empire.

bactria.name: Bactria
bactria.summary: An ancient Iranian region of Central Asia between the Oxus River and the Hindu Kush, an early centre of Zoroastrianism later ruled by the Achaemenid Empire and conquered by Alexander the Great.

sogdia.name: Sogdia
sogdia.summary: An ancient Iranian civilisation between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, conquered in turn by Persian, Greek and other empires; its merchants were key middlemen on the Silk Road.

mithraism.name: Mithraism
mithraism.summary: A Roman mystery religion centered on the god Mithras, popular in the Imperial army from the 1st to 4th centuries CE, with initiates meeting in underground temples called mithraea.

mandaeism.name: Mandaeism
mandaeism.summary: A Gnostic, monotheistic religion shaped by Greek, Iranian and Jewish influences, whose followers revere figures like Adam and Noah and regard John the Baptist as their greatest and final prophet.

manichaeism.name: Manichaeism
manichaeism.summary: A major dualistic religion founded in the 3rd century CE by the prophet Mani, teaching a cosmic struggle between light and darkness and drawing on Zoroastrian, Christian and Buddhist traditions.

mani-prophet.name: Mani
mani-prophet.summary: An Iranian prophet (c. 216–274 CE) who founded Manichaeism, born near Ctesiphon in the Parthian Empire and later imprisoned and killed under the Sasanian ruler Bahram I.

yasht.name: Yashts
yasht.summary: A Middle Persian term for sacrifice or worship, most often applied to a collection of 21 hymns within the Avesta, Zoroastrianism's sacred texts.

yasna.name: Yasna
yasna.summary: Both a text within the Avesta and the principal act of worship in Zoroastrianism.

proto-indo-iranian-religion.name: Proto-Indo-Iranian religion
proto-indo-iranian-religion.summary: The reconstructed religion of the early Indo-Iranian peoples, including concepts like universal order (rta/asha) and the sacred drink soma/haoma, ancestral to later Iranian and Indo-Aryan religions.

sasanian-empire.name: Sasanian Empire
sasanian-empire.summary: An Iranian empire ruled by the House of Sasan from 224 to 651 AD, founded by Ardashir I to revive the legacy of the Achaemenid Empire; at its height it stretched from Egypt to Central Asia.

muslim-conquest-of-persia.name: Muslim conquest of Persia
muslim-conquest-of-persia.summary: A military campaign in which the Rashidun Caliphate conquered the Sasanian Empire between 633 and 651 CE, part of the early Muslim conquests that began under Muhammad in 627/628.
